catalog_quote: In Koch the phonetic correlate of stress is a combination of length and loudness. Koch stress is phonologically predictable: in simple words it invariably falls on the last syllable from the end as in: bʰɛˈda ‘water lily’, ɾaˈd͡ʒa ‘king’, kʰɔjtɔˈblɛŋ ‘bulbul’. Words with inflectional suffixes carry stress in two places – one on the last syllable of the root and the other on the last syllable of the suffix as in: hut͡ʃˈuŋ-aˈ-na ‘turtle-DEF-ACC’ > ‘the turtle’. In compound words (including proper nouns) or those derived from two roots there are also stress in two places as in: pʰɛˈpɔɾaˈd͡ʒa ‘Snake King’. The nature of double stress in the latter two cases needs further investigation as there are polysyllabic words with longer roots as well as the roots followed by more than two suffixes.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (300-page volume; the PDF's metadata gives the title "NEIL7-master-2015-FINAL"). PDF page 39 = printed p. 35, running head "2. Harigaya Koch phonology", sections "5. Suprasegmental phonology / 5.1. Stress / 5.2. Contrastive pitch". The text garbles IPA, so I rendered the page to PNG and read it: the quoted passage is there verbatim, and the IPA examples match the report exactly (bʰɛˈda 'water lily', ɾaˈd͡ʒa 'king', kʰɔjtɔˈblɛŋ 'bulbul'; hut͡ʃˈuŋ-aˈ-na 'turtle-DEF-ACC'; pʰɛˈpɔɾaˈd͡ʒa 'Snake King'), followed by the "nature of double stress.. needs further investigation" sentence. §5.2 on the same page: "Koch is one among a few Boro-Garo languages that have abandoned tone", with high pi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and word-final: in a simple (monomorphemic) word it always falls on the last syllable. When inflectional suffixes are added, the word carries two stresses, one on the last syllable of the root and one on the last syllable of the suffix string; compounds and two-root derivatives likewise get a stress on the final syllable of each member. Stress is cued by length plus loudness; there is no vowel-length contrast and no lexical tone (only a lexicalized high pitch on a few demonstratives).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as secondary. The author speaks of 'double stress' (two stresses) in suffixed and compound words and says its nature 'needs further investigation as there are polysyllabic words with longer roots as well as the roots followed by more than two suffixes' (p. 35); the 2020 sketch (p. 25) lists 'the nature of stress in polysyllabic words' as an open question.
new_statements.exceptions: None for simple words ('invariably'). Suffixed and compound words are the stated departure (two stresses). §5.2 notes contrastive high pitch + length lexicalized in a few demonstratives (ũaŋ 'there' vs ú:aŋ 'over there'), described as pitch, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation/elicited forms (about 1,000 phonemicized words collected 2008-2009). Harigaya variety only; the author says Koch, like Garo, 'lacks contrastive tones' and calls the syllable the key phonological unit.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for the Harigaya variety of Koch [kdq] (West Garo Hills, Meghalaya), the central lingua-franca variety; Glottolog koch1250 has no separate dialect codes. Kondakov 2015/2020 treat Koch as toneless. The only other opened description, Shaikh 2022 (University of Hyderabad thesis), describes the Koch of Alipurduar/Jalpaiguri/Cooch Behar districts, West Bengal, gives no stress rule and claims two lexical tones (high/low) with minimal pairs (pp. 111-113); that is a different variety and a contradictory analysis, so the catalog entry should be labelled Harigaya Koch (Kondakov) and the tone claim flagged as variety-specific/unverified.

sources.note: §5.1 Stress (p. 35): stress = length + loudness; phonologically predictable, in simple words invariably on the last syllable; suffixed words carry stress on the last syllable of the root and on the last syllable of the suffix; compounds/two-root words also have two stresses; 'nature of double stress.. needs further investigation'. §5.2: Koch has abandoned tone, but high pitch + length is lexicalized in a few demonstratives (u ~ ú: 'there/over there').

sources.note: §2.7 Stress (pp. 4-5) repeats the 2015 statement verbatim: predictable final stress in simple words (bʰɛˈda, ɾaˈd͡ʒa, kʰɔjtɔˈblɛŋ); two stresses in suffixed words (hut͡ʃˈuŋ-aˈ-na) and in compound nouns (maˈma-bhagiˈnə); double stress needs further study. §2.2: no vowel length contrast, a stressed vowel is slightly longer. §2.3: no contrastive tone. Conclusion (p. 25) lists 'the nature of stress in polysyllabic words' as open.

sources.citation: Shaikh, Rahamat. 2022. A Descriptive Grammar of Koch. PhD thesis, Centre for Endangered Languages & Mother Tongue Studies, University of Hyderabad (supervisor Panchanan Mohanty). 280 pp. Shodhganga handle 10603/480048
sources.note: Chapter IV gives no rule for word-stress placement; the only occurrence of 'stress' is a generic textbook definition of falling vs rising diphthongs. §4.12 'Tones in Koch' (pp. 111-113) claims Koch is a tone language with two tones (high vs low) and lists ~18 minimal pairs (e.g. sɯ́m 'beg' / sɯ̀m 'salt'). Data are from Koch speakers of Alipurduar, Jalpaiguri and Cooch Behar districts, West Bengal (ch. 1) — a different variety from Kondakov's Harigaya, and the tone claim contradicts Kondakov's 'no tone'.
